title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

analysis.problem_summary: Remove the n-th node from the end of a singly linked list and return the head of the modified list.
analysis.intuition: The n-th node from the end is at a distance of len - n steps from the start of the list. Since a singly linked list can only be traversed forward, we can first make a full pass to count the total length of the list. In a second pass, we navigate to the node immediately before the target node to bypass it. Creating a dummy node pointing to the head simplifies edge cases—specifically when the node to be removed is the head itself (when len == n)—because the dummy node acts as a permanent predecessor.
approach: Initialize a counter len = 0 and a pointer cur = head.
Traverse the linked list using cur, incrementing len until cur becomes null to compute the total node count.
Instantiate a dummy node with value 0 and set dummy.next = head to handle head deletions cleanly.
Compute jumps = len - n, which represents the number of forward steps required from dummy to reach the node preceding the target.
Initialize prev = dummy and advance prev forward jumps times using a loop.
Unlink the target node by reassigning prev.next = prev.next.next.
Return dummy.next, which holds the head of the updated list.
analysis.why_it_works: In a list of total length `len`, the n-th node from the end is located at 0-based index `len - n` relative to the head. Starting from a dummy node positioned before the head, advancing `len - n` steps stops exactly at the predecessor node (index `len - n - 1` relative to head). Modifying `prev.next` to point to `prev.next.next` effectively unlinks the target node without altering any other links in the list.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using a dummy node placed before the head simplifies linked list node deletions by ensuring every node, including the original head, has a valid predecessor to update.
analysis.time_explanation: The list is traversed twice—once to measure its total length N and once to reach the removal point—taking O(N) linear time overall.
analysis.space_explanation: The implementation only allocates a single dummy node and a few pointer variables, requiring O(1) auxiliary space.

analysis.problem_summary: Remove the nth node from the end of a singly-linked list in a single pass.
analysis.intuition: Maintaining a fixed gap of n nodes between a fast pointer and a slow pointer allows us to find the node preceding the target when the fast pointer reaches the end.
approach: Advance a fast pointer cur forward by n steps from the head.
Create a dummy head node pointing to head and place a slow pointer prev at dummy.
Advance both cur and prev simultaneously one step at a time until cur reaches null.
Update prev.next = prev.next.next to remove the target node and return dummy.next.
analysis.why_it_works: Because the distance between cur and prev is exactly n + 1 nodes (due to prev starting at dummy), when cur reaches null (end of list at position L + 1 relative to dummy), prev rests exactly at position L - n, which is the node right before the target.
analysis.key_takeaway: Maintaining a fixed offset window with two pointers eliminates the need to pre-compute the list length and achieves single-pass execution.
analysis.time_explanation: The fast pointer traverses the list of length N exactly once, performing the entire operation in O(N) time.
analysis.space_explanation: Only pointer references and a single dummy node are maintained, requiring O(1) auxiliary space.
